Remember this distinction: Archivists preserve records and make them discoverable, while librarians lend resources and help people understand them. Both organize information, but their materials differ.

This career is a poor fit for people who dislike repetitive detail, cannot sustain quiet work, or need fast feedback. Description, conservation, and reference services take substantial time and offer little glamour.

A common path is: degree in archives, library and information science, history, or a related field → archival assistant → description and conservation training → responsibility for a record group → collections or digital archivist.

This career suits careful, quiet, organized people with patience for documents and history. Treating long-term preservation and reliable access as meaningful outcomes creates a stable foundation for the work.

Archivists (Archivists) receive, appraise, arrange, describe, preserve, and provide access to records with lasting value. They maintain authenticity and traceability as guardians of organizational memory and cultural heritage.

paragraphs: The morning starts in the repository, accessioning new records and performing cleaning and disinfection. In the afternoon, the archivist describes and digitizes materials and checks metadata item by item. Research requests require finding-aid searches, retrieval, and checkout records. Restoring old film involves careful work under a light table while wearing gloves.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 9,300 Archivists were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to reach 9,700 by 2034, a net gain of about 400 jobs, with roughly 1,100 openings each year. Median annual pay was about $61,600 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

paragraphs: A 6/10 score places this career in the moderate exposure range for cataloging and retrieval. Systems accelerate data entry and search, while appraisal and preservation remain human-led.

Moderate exposure does not mean high career risk. AI replaces transcription and retrieval, not value appraisal. Archivists with digital preservation and curatorial skills become more scarce. Junior roles based only on mechanical description face the greatest pressure.

Build a foundation in archives, library and information science, or history, and study digital technology and descriptive standards. The AI era rewards appraisal and preservation skills, not data entry alone.
Expand from physical collections into digital archives. Learn data governance and long-term preservation, master OCR and search tools, and develop into a digital archivist with curatorial skills.
Highlight the record groups you managed, digitization projects you completed, and standards you know. Digital preservation experience receives priority.

Archivists emphasize preservation and evidence. They manage original records and protect their integrity. Librarians emphasize lending and reading and manage publications. One preserves memory, while the other enables reading.

AI will not replace the profession as a whole, but it will reshape arrangement and description. As OCR and automated description take over data entry, archivists shift toward appraisal, digital preservation, and curation. Professionals who protect long-term preservation remain more secure.
Value appraisal, protection of authenticity, conservation decisions, curatorial narrative, archival security, and accountability for loss.

Archivists mainly work in public archives, libraries, universities, research institutes, and archives or knowledge-management departments at large companies. Work alternates between quiet, controlled repositories and offices.

The career remains worthwhile with the right direction. Pure cataloging is contracting, while value is shifting toward digital preservation and data governance. Treat it as a deep specialty, learn digital technology and curation while working, and build long-term stability through experience.
